title: 2 Chronicles 7:11–22
context: 2 Chronicles 7:11–22 records the LORD’s second appearance to Solomon by night, answering the dedication prayer of chapter 6. God says he has chosen the temple as a house of sacrifice. If he shuts the sky, sends locusts, or sends pestilence, and his people who are called by his name humble themselves, pray, seek his face, and turn from their wicked ways, he will hear, forgive, and heal their land. These verses (7:13–15), which are not in the parallel at 1 Kings 9:1–9, answer the specific requests of Solomon’s prayer about drought, locusts, and plague (6:26–31). Verse 14 is a promise to Israel in the setting of the temple and the covenant, not a general slogan, though Christians in both traditions draw from it the lasting truth that God hears the humble and repentant. God then promises to establish Solomon’s throne if he walks as David did, and warns that if Israel turns to other gods, he will uproot them from the land and make the temple a byword. As in the drafted notes on 1 Kings 9:1–9, both traditions read the passage as shared ground about God’s presence, repentance, and the real threat of judgment.

verses.text: Thus Solomon finished the LORD’s house and the king’s house; and he successfully completed all that came into Solomon’s heart to make in the LORD’s house and in his own house.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon finishes the LORD’s house and his own house and completes all he had in mind. Arminian readers see faithful work brought to completion, and they note the parallel in 1 Kings 9:1.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s blessing enabling Solomon to finish the work. Both traditions read the verse as setting the stage for God’s response to the dedication prayer.

verses.text: Then the LORD appeared to Solomon by night, and said to him, “I have heard your prayer, and have chosen this place for myself for a house of sacrifice.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD appears to Solomon by night and says he has heard his prayer and chosen the temple as a house of sacrifice. Arminians see God personally answering the prayer of chapter 6, which shows that he listens to his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress God’s choice of the place for his worship. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: God hears prayer and appoints the means by which his people approach him.

verses.text: “If I shut up the sky so that there is no rain, or if I command the locust to devour the land, or if I send pestilence among my people,
verses.arminianNotes: God speaks of shutting the sky, sending locusts, or sending pestilence among his people. Arminian readers see these as disciplines God might send in response to sin, matching the requests in Solomon’s prayer (6:26–28).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over nature used to call his people back. Both traditions read the verse in the setting of the covenant, where such disasters are linked with Israel’s unfaithfulness, and they avoid applying it mechanically to every calamity.

verses.text: if my people who are called by my name will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
verses.arminianNotes: If God’s people who are called by his name humble themselves, pray, seek his face, and turn from their wicked ways, he will hear, forgive, and heal their land. Arminian readers see a sincere, conditional promise to Israel that calls for a real turning, and they see God’s readiness to forgive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the promise is real and conditional in form, and they add that God himself works the humility he calls for. Both traditions read the verse first in its temple and covenant setting, not as a generic slogan, while drawing from it the lasting truth that God hears the repentant.

verses.text: Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to prayer that is made in this place.
verses.arminianNotes: God says his eyes will be open and his ears attentive to prayer made in this place. Arminians see God’s promise to listen as encouraging his people to come to him in prayer, as Solomon had asked (6:40).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the promise as God’s gracious commitment to his people. Both traditions note that for Christians, Jesus becomes the place where God meets his people (John 2:19–21), while reading the verse first in its own setting.

verses.text: For now I have chosen and made this house holy, that my name may be there forever; and my eyes and my heart will be there perpetually.
verses.arminianNotes: God has chosen and made the house holy, so that his name, eyes, and heart will be there perpetually. Arminian readers see God’s lasting commitment to dwell among his people, and they see the promise held within the covenant warnings that follow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress God’s own choice and consecration of the temple. Both traditions note that the warning in 7:19–22 shows the temple’s continuance was tied to Israel’s faithfulness, which is shared ground.

verses.text: “As for you, if you will walk before me as David your father walked, and do according to all that I have commanded you, and will keep my statutes and my ordinances,
verses.arminianNotes: God tells Solomon that if he walks before him as David did and keeps his commandments, statutes, and ordinances, the following promise will apply. Arminians see a real call to faithful obedience that has real consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the call to obedience as the fitting response to God’s grace. Both traditions read the conditional form as genuine, consistent with the drafted notes on 1 Kings 9:4.

verses.text: then I will establish the throne of your kingdom, according as I covenanted with David your father, saying, ‘There shall not fail you a man to be ruler in Israel.’
verses.arminianNotes: God promises to establish Solomon’s throne as he covenanted with David, that a man to rule in Israel would not fail him. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness to the covenant with David, and they note that 1 Kings 9:5 speaks of a man on the throne of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and name the difference in wording without harmonizing it. Both traditions see the promise to David (2 Samuel 7:12–16) as ultimately fulfilled in Christ, while reading the verse first in Solomon’s setting.

verses.text: But if you turn away and forsake my statutes and my commandments which I have set before you, and go and serve other gods and worship them,
verses.arminianNotes: God warns that if they turn away, forsake his commandments, and serve other gods, consequences will follow. Arminians see the warning as genuine, showing that the people could truly turn from God and face judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the warning is real and serious, and they see it as one of the means God uses to keep his people faithful. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the danger of idolatry.

verses.text: then I will pluck them up by the roots out of my land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, I will cast out of my sight, and I will make it a proverb and a byword among all peoples.
verses.arminianNotes: God says he will uproot them from the land and cast the temple out of his sight, making it a proverb and a byword. Arminian readers see the seriousness of covenant unfaithfulness, which could lead even to losing the land and the temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that this warning was fulfilled in the exile (2 Chronicles 36). Both traditions read the verse as a sober reminder that God’s presence among his people does not protect them from judgment if they abandon him.

verses.text: This house, which is so high, everyone who passes by it will be astonished and say, ‘Why has the LORD done this to this land and to this house?’
verses.arminianNotes: Everyone who passes the ruined temple will be astonished and ask why the LORD has done this. Arminians see the ruin becoming a public lesson about the results of turning from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the question as leading to a confession of God’s justice. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 9:8 and with Deuteronomy 29:24, which describes a similar question.

verses.text: They shall answer, ‘Because they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and took other gods, worshiped them, and served them. Therefore he has brought all this evil on them.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The answer will be that they abandoned the LORD, who brought them out of Egypt, and served other gods, so he brought this evil on them. Arminian readers see judgment as the just result of abandoning the God who redeemed them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice in the judgment. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: God’s past redemption makes unfaithfulness more serious, and his judgment is a response to persistent idolatry.
